sources.title: Monuments, Sites and Cultural Landscape of Chiang Mai, Capital of Lanna
sources.note: Thailand nomination dossier describes long cultural continuity, diverse communities, temples, writing, trade, waterworks, war damage, dispersal, and Kawila-era revival.

sources.title: History of Lan Na by Sarassawadee Ongsakul, Chulalongkorn University catalog
sources.note: University catalog outlines distinct phases: kingdom, Burmese rule from 1558 to 1774, then Siamese tributary status, with society and economy treated separately.

sources.title: Ken Kirigaya, Lan Na under Burma: A Dark Age in Northern Thailand?
sources.note: Source-critical political and social history challenges a uniform dark-age story; details local rulers, trade, taxation, warfare, religious patronage, writing, and chronology.

sources.title: Latdawan Sae-Siao, Lan Na politics under Burmese rule, English abstract
sources.note: Chiang Mai University thesis abstract distinguishes local autonomy, tighter post-1664 administration, economic extraction, local leadership, and the 1774 alliance with Thonburi.

sources.title: Ken Kirigaya, Some Annotations to the Chiang Mai Chronicle
sources.note: Cross-checks Lan Na, Burmese, and inscriptional chronologies; documents 1630s patronage, novice ordinations, local dignitaries, and common scribal or identification errors.

sources.title: Wat Pang Mo Puang Buddha-base inscription, SAC database
sources.note: Official Thai inscription record dates a Tai Tham text to 1612 at Chiang Saen and identifies a male donor, his wife, and other merit makers.

sources.title: Wat Selarattanapapphataram old wooden inscription, SAC database
sources.note: Official record dates a five-line Tai Tham inscription to 1683 at Wat Lai Hin and quotes its calendrical opening in normalized Thai transcription.

sources.title: Apiradee Techasiriwan and Volker Grabowsky, Multi-scriptural and Multilingual Inscriptions in Lan Na
sources.note: Academic inscription study shows Tai Yuan, Pali, Tai Tham, Fak Kham, and Burmese choices, including bilingual political and devotional objects under Burmese rule.

sources.title: Digital Library of Northern Thai Manuscripts resources
sources.note: Institutional resource explains Tham-script history, catalog methods, languages, titles, dating, and the 1471 oldest securely dated manuscript.

sources.title: SOAS announcement for the Digital Library of Northern Thai Manuscripts
sources.note: Institutional account describes four digitized collections and Northern Thai, Pali, Tai Khuen, Tai Lue, Lao, Shan, and Burmese manuscript holdings.

sources.title: Review of Lan Na Literature catalog, Journal of the Siam Society 75
sources.note: Reviews a catalog of 3,700 microfilmed manuscripts, including 954 secular works on ethics, chronicles, divination, poetry, medicine, magic, and everyday rites.

sources.title: Harald Hundius, Buddhist Literature of Lan Na
sources.note: Philological survey inventories inscriptions and palm-leaf literature, including a dated 1605 Chiang Saen bronze inscription and the limits of literary classification.

sources.title: Prhamaha Worachet Aunren, Rights of Phrai in Mangraisat Customary Law
sources.note: Chiang Mai University study describes family, marriage, inheritance, land, irrigation, labor, travel, appeal, and wartime protections in a transmitted Lan Na law text.

sources.title: Pakdeekul Ratana, The Role of Lan Na Women in Historical Perspective
sources.note: Chiang Mai University author synthesizes inscriptions, law, chronicles, and literature to describe historically changing and active women’s economic and social roles.

sources.title: A Study on Lanna Ways of Life and Beliefs from Lanna Inscriptions
sources.note: Silpakorn University thesis studies 186 inscriptions from 1279 to 1935, including merit, land donation, temple labor, family consent, and debt, while spanning many periods.

sources.title: Richard Davis, Muang Matrifocality
sources.note: Later ethnography documents initial matrilocal residence, matriclans, household sleeping arrangements, and regional variation; useful only as a bounded comparison.

sources.title: Sanguan Chotisukharat, Supernatural Beliefs and Practices in Chiengmai
sources.note: Later rural account describes evening courtship, weaving and other work, parental presence, verbal artistry, and spirit placation; not direct seventeenth-century evidence.

sources.title: Vanpen Surarerks, Muang Fai Communities in Northern Thailand
sources.note: Peer-reviewed study identifies centuries-old communal weirs, canals, agreements, committees, fees, maintenance labor, and negotiated water distribution in northern Thailand.

sources.title: SAC archaeology database: ancient Chiang Mai
sources.note: Official archaeological site record describes city walls, moats, Mae Kha drainage, terrain, water, transport, temple landscape, war, and later restoration.

sources.title: The Plan of Chiang Mai City: Concepts and Local Knowledge
sources.note: Research on city planning discusses earthworks, moat water, cosmology, environmental knowledge, and the relationship between settlement and hydrology.

sources.title: Smithsonian, Ceramics in Mainland Southeast Asia: Lan Na
sources.note: Smithsonian research database notes debate over kiln decline after 1558 and evidence that Kalong production may have continued into the seventeenth century.

sources.title: Narong Sikhiram, Food Culture in Lanna Way of Life
sources.note: Modern qualitative study identifies sticky rice, chili pastes, local vegetables, cooking methods, medicinal ideas, and historical influence; used as later continuity, not direct proof.

sources.title: Kamthieng House Museum, Siam Society
sources.note: Museum describes a mid-nineteenth-century northern Thai teak house inherited through a matrilineal clan; explicitly later than the card interval.

sources.title: James Mulholland, Thai Traditional Medicine: Ancient Thought and Practice
sources.note: Historical review explains manuscript transmission, remedies, massage diagrams, pharmacy, later compilations, and why preserved texts do not equal measured clinical outcomes.

sources.title: Buddhist palm-leaf manuscripts in the reign of King Kawila
sources.note: Study of eight late eighteenth and early nineteenth-century bundles describes daylight writing, team production, named monks and laypeople, merit, pedagogy, and recovery.

sources.title: Review of the Chiang Mai Chronicle, Journal of the Siam Society
sources.note: Review dates the surviving expanded version around 1827 to 1828 and explains its layered relationship to earlier versions and Lan Na historical memory.

sources.title: Donald Swearer, Myth, Legend and History in the Northern Thai Chronicles
sources.note: Study explains religious and legendary framing in northern chronicles, warning against reading every narrative element as a simple eyewitness report.

sources.title: Chiang Mai University study of Chronicle narratives and Kawila
sources.note: University article separates Burmese rule, local resistance, Thonburi aid, Kawila’s appointment, ritual re-entry, and later narrative elaboration.

sources.title: Recognition of Muang Fai water-management customary law
sources.note: Legal study explains the weir-and-ditch technology and its simultaneous role as water, social, and organizational management.

sources.title: Natural Degradation of Earthworks, Trenches, Walls and Moats, Northern Thailand
sources.note: Archaeological study examines northern Thai earthworks and Chiang Saen brick wall and moat, emphasizing preservation and landscape processes rather than timeless form.

sources.title: Queensland Art Gallery, Bust of the Buddha
sources.note: Museum collection note describes sophisticated Lan Na bronze production and stylistic exchange while acknowledging broad art-historical dating.

sources.title: Cherdsak Treerayapiwat, hierarchy of ancient Lan Na communities
sources.note: Chiang Mai University geography thesis combines archaeology, GIS, archives, and central-place analysis to distinguish ranked settlement units in Chiang Mai and Lamphun.

sources.title: Anan Ganjanapan, directions in the study of Lan Na history and society
sources.note: Historiographical review stresses cultural diversity, social change, multiple ethnic settlements, and the limitations of older static pictures of northern society.

sources.title: Volker Grabowsky, The Northern Tai Polity of Lan Na
sources.note: National University of Singapore working paper uses indigenous and Chinese evidence to show rival regional centers, tributary relations, overland trade, and why a unitary-kingdom image misleads.

sources.title: Xu Qianqian and Sarassawadee Ongsakul, Chin-Ho merchants between Lan Na and Yunnan
sources.note: Peer-reviewed study identifies Hui caravan merchants, mules and horses, and connected mainland routes between Yunnan and Lan Na through the seventeenth century.

sources.title: Saiklang Jindasu, From Highland to Maritime Trade
sources.note: Thailand Fine Arts Department volume documents seventeenth-century Chiang Mai demand for upland products, foreign merchants, natural-resource exports, and Lan Na intermediaries.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Interwoven Globe trade timeline
sources.note: Museum research timeline records an East India Company agent reaching Chiang Mai in 1613 to 1623 with Coromandel cloth for gold, rubies, benzoin, wax, and deerskins.

sources.title: Than Tun, The Royal Orders of Burma, summary volume
sources.note: Digitized primary-source corpus and editorial summary documents Burmese administrative categories for tolls, ferries, ports, markets, brokerage, customary dues, and official limits on collections.

sources.title: Edoardo Siani, The City Stabilized: The Kawila Restoration
sources.note: Open-access university-press chapter studies Chiang Mai after the wars, gradual Kawila-era restoration, local authority under Siamese tributary relations, and remembered urban space.

sources.title: Volker Grabowsky, Population Dynamics in Lan Na during the Nineteenth Century
sources.note: Demographic history traces political fragmentation, warfare, depopulation, forced migration, the 1775 rupture, and the long restoration ending at Chiang Saen in 1804.
